In the Court of Common Pleas · Knox County, Ohio

The Knox Cattle Dam Case

State of Ohio, ex rel. Dave Yost, Attorney GeneralPlaintiff · at the request of ODNR
— v. —
The Landings Property Owners Association, Inc., Mullins Bros. Ltd., the City of Mount Vernon, and the lot owners of Phases VII & VIII, et al.Defendants & third-party defendants
FILED JUNE 2020JUDGE RICHARD D. WETZELYAUGER ROAD · MOUNT VERNON

Case brief · updated September 14, 2026

Summary of the Litigation

I. Question Presented

Who owns — and who must pay to repair and maintain — the Knox Cattle Company Dam, a 1945 earthen embankment on Yauger Road in Mount Vernon that has been out of compliance with Ohio's dam-safety laws since at least 2008?

II. Background

The dam impounds the lake behind The Landings development. ODNR inspections in 2008, 2010, 2015, and 2020 documented safety violations; after homes were approved and built below the dam, ODNR reclassified it from Class II to Class I (high hazard), a standard the structure was never built to meet. The ownership question surfaced publicly in 2019 during Mount Vernon's storm-water utility discussions. In June 2020 the Ohio Attorney General, at ODNR's request, filed suit in Knox County Common Pleas asking the court to declare the dam's legal owner and compel compliance. Defendants included The Landings Property Owners Association, Inc. (a POA whose articles of incorporation were cancelled in 2015), developer Mullins Bros. Ltd., Delano Asset Management, Crown Hill Condominiums, the City of Mount Vernon, and nearby homeowners.

Mullins Bros. brought third-party claims against the roughly 68 lot owners of Landings Phases VII and VIII — including Matt & Megan Snow — contending that the recorded Declarations of Building and Development Restrictions obligated lot owners to join a homeowners association with "sole and exclusive control of the lake … and responsib[ility] for its care and maintenance." The Phase VII/VIII owners retained Stephen E. Chappelear of Eastman & Smith Ltd., with neighbor Mark Long serving as group liaison.

III. Procedural History

Judge Richard Wetzel initially recused himself (his wife worked at an involved property), and visiting Judge James Kimbler dismissed Waters Edge, Delano, and 24 Mallard Pointe owners in March 2023 while signaling that Phase VII/VIII owners could be added. Then, on June 25, 2024, the Supreme Court of Ohio rescinded Kimbler's assignment and the case returned to Judge Wetzel, who had told the Supreme Court his conflict "has abated." The group viewed this as the moment momentum was lost: Kimbler had been deciding the case on dam-ownership law, while Wetzel had leaned toward mediation, and three months after his return Wetzel issued the ruling that made the homeowners members of the owning corporation. Members raised removing him again, and were still raising it in 2025; counsel never moved to disqualify.

Through 2023 the parties took discovery: requests for admission and production, and four depositions (Steve Mullins twice, his attorney Bob Rauzi, and Cloyd Yough). In December 2023 the homeowners and Mullins Bros. filed cross-motions for summary judgment. The homeowners argued that only an owner of a dam bears the statutory duty to repair it; that they do not own it; and that the Declarations gave inadequate notice, impose no individual liability, and speak to the "lake," not the dam. Briefing closed in early 2024, followed by two rounds of supplemental memoranda answering the court's questions — including the homeowners' argument that the 1990s quitclaim transfer to the defunct POA should be set aside for lack of ODNR approval.

Key ruling — Decision & Entry, September 23, 2024
  1. The individual landowners do not own the dam.
  2. The owner is The Landings Property Owners Association, Inc. — the POA cancelled in 2015.
  3. A receiver would be appointed to act for the defunct corporation, subject to ODNR approval.
  4. Phase VII & VIII residents are bound by the recorded Declarations, which require membership in the association responsible for care and maintenance of the lake — and "the lake" includes the dam.
  5. Who pays for remediation and ongoing expenses was left for trial.

On October 3–4, 2024 the court appointed Jack Harris of Intercept Management Corp. as receiver, with seven ordered tasks: encumber the county's ~$900,000 in remaining ARPA funds before the year-end deadline, coordinate interim risk-reduction work, organize a functioning HOA under the Declarations, and determine assessments on the Phase VII/VIII lot owners. Monthly telephone status conferences (last Friday of each month) have run ever since.

IV. The Repair

The City led the interim risk-reduction work, hiring AK Hydro (roughly $200,000 — half of Stantec's bid) with work beginning after July 1, 2025 per ODNR. In July 2025 the receiver's Sixth Report priced three permanent alternatives; he recommended Option 3 (~$710,000) — reshaping the impoundment so capacity drops below 15 acre-feet, removing the dam from ODNR jurisdiction, with the cost covered by the county's $1M ARPA award. A public meeting at the Woodward Opera House on August 20, 2025 presented the options. Cost estimates then grew, and the plan evolved into a "Two-Pond Option" (two ponds separated by a causeway). Over the group's objection — Chappelear argued for the cheaper Single-Pond option, citing up to $200,000 in change-order risk — Judge Wetzel approved the Two-Pond plan on November 12, 2025.

Construction by Haynes Construction ran ahead of schedule through summer 2026 and was substantially complete by August 2026 (seeding in September), within the available federal funds. Funding backstop: a Park National Bank loan committed by seven pond-frontage owners. Ongoing maintenance (~$30,000/year, escalating ~3%) is to be spread across roughly 200 parcels — The Landings, Mallard Point, Water's Edge, Coventry Court, and the KCH offices on Woodlake Trail — at an estimated $150–200 per parcel per year, collected via City water bills. ODNR will inspect and ultimately sign the project over to the POA.

V. Current Posture (September 2026)

On September 8, 2026, Eastman & Smith terminated its representation of the homeowner group, citing an inability to get direction from group representatives (one moving out of state, another stepping away) and some members' refusal to pay fees. On September 14 the firm filed its Motion to Withdraw as Counsel with the court. A "Legal Representation Reboot" led by Mark Long briefly explored keeping Eastman & Smith for the remaining work, but the firm withdrew anyway; as of September 14, 23 households (20+ owners) — including the Snows — have signed on to seek substitute counsel, ideally an attorney already in the case, before the September 25 status conference. Chappelear's parting letter flags the open issues:

  • The court-recognized HOA (the Landings POA) exists and all Phase VII/VIII owners are members; the receiver will impose bylaws, governance, and dues if owners don't organize their own.
  • A pending receiver motion to approve assessments: a $45,000 one-time vegetation-clearing assessment and a monthly maintenance assessment — with open questions about reasonableness and allocation.
  • Counsel's warning that the receiver "is not a fiduciary with any duties to the lot owners" and has aligned with City interests.
  • Unresolved claims reserved for trial: indemnity and contribution, injunctive relief, Water Pollution Control Act violations, and breach of the Declarations.
  • Monthly status calls continue — next on September 25, 2026, 11:00 a.m.
"Whether you like the lawsuit or not … there are realities that cannot be ignored, and the lawsuit is not going away by simply wishing it were so."— Stephen E. Chappelear, termination letter, Sept. 8, 2026

Scorecard · as of September 14, 2026

What's Decided, What's Not

A. Is there still a suit against us?

Yes. The case (20IN06-0149) remains pending, and every Phase VII/VIII lot owner is still a defendant/third-party defendant — the court has twice refused to dismiss the homeowners, even after finding they don't individually own the dam. Selling a home does not remove an owner from the case (it takes a court-approved substitution of the buyer). What has changed is the shape of the exposure: the repair itself was paid from federal funds, so the live risk is no longer a six-figure construction bill — it is assessments (vegetation clearing and ongoing maintenance) imposed through the court-recognized HOA, plus the claims the court expressly reserved for trial (indemnity and contribution, injunctive relief, Water Pollution Control Act violations, breach of the Declarations). No trial date has been set, and no money judgment has been entered against any homeowner.

B. Decisions by the court — and the court's reasoning

Decided · Sept. 23, 2024 — individual owners do not own the dam

No deed conveys the dam parcel to any Phase VII/VIII lot owner, and under Ohio dam-safety law only an owner bears the duty to repair and maintain a dam. This was the defense's central argument, and the court accepted it — it is why no homeowner has been held personally to own the structure.

Decided · Sept. 23, 2024 — The Landings POA, Inc. owns the dam

The dam/lake parcel was quitclaimed by the developer to The Landings Property Owners Association, Inc. in the 1990s. The group argued the transfer should be set aside — the POA was never validly formed and ODNR never approved the transfer — but the court let the deed stand and placed ownership on the (defunct) corporation rather than returning it to Mullins Bros.

Decided · Sept. 23, 2024 — Phase VII/VIII owners are bound by the Declarations

The Declarations of Building and Development Restrictions were recorded with the County Recorder, which the court treated as binding notice to every lot buyer. The court held them "enforceable against the Developer, Mullins Bros., and the respective lot owners," said it "will enforce the Declaration of Restrictions by further orders," and enjoined any amendment without court approval. The defense arguments — inadequate notice, no individual liability, and that the Declarations mention only the "lake" — were rejected: the court read the required membership in the "Landings Common Area Association" as a misnomer for the POA, and held that control and maintenance of the lake necessarily includes the dam that impounds it.

Where the misnomer finding came from. The Declarations require owners to join the "Landings Common Area Association, Inc." — a different entity from "The Landings Property Owners Association, Inc." named on the deed. That gap was the group's best textual argument, and Mullins Bros. closed it by deposing its own former attorney, Robert Rauzi, who drafted both documents. On September 7, 2023 Rauzi testified the mismatch was his own drafting error — a "scrivener's error" a court could correct in equity. Chappelear reported at the time that he did not believe the facts supported that approach; a year later the court adopted it. That transcript is the evidentiary hinge of the whole case.

Decided · Oct. 4, 2024 — receivership

Because the owning corporation had been defunct since 2015, someone had to act for it. Jack Harris (Intercept Management Corp.) was appointed with seven ordered tasks: encumber the county's ARPA funds before the federal deadline, remediate the dam subject to ODNR approval, organize a functioning HOA under the Declarations and the Revised Code, and determine assessments on Phase VII/VIII owners, collected through a City mechanism.

Decided · Nov. 12, 2025 — the Two-Pond repair plan

Choosing between the receiver's Two-Pond option and the group's cheaper Single-Pond alternative, the court ordered a supplemental engineering report and then followed AK Hydro's opinion on flood risk and safety — approving Two-Pond over the group's cost objection. The construction was completed in 2026 within the available federal funds, mooting the change-order fear in practice.

Effectively resolved (not by verdict, but by events)
  1. The dam is fixed. Construction substantially complete Aug. 2026, within the county's $1M ARPA award — no construction balance falls on homeowners. ODNR inspection and sign-over to the POA remain.
  2. Regulatory exposure shrinks. The rebuilt configuration reduces capacity below ODNR's jurisdictional threshold.
  3. Funding backstop in place. A Park National Bank loan committed by seven pond-frontage owners covers any shortfall.

C. Still outstanding — before the court or in the receiver's hands

  • Forming the HOA. The court says the HOA already exists — the Landings POA, with all Phase VII/VIII owners as members. What's unfinished is making it real: the receiver's draft bylaws (revisions requested, response pending), the Notice of Amendment to the Declarations filed July 2026, choosing directors and officers from the neighborhood, and setting dues. A six-member owner council (Long, Marlow, Rhoades, Belcher, Goodrich, Varughese) has volunteered to work these with the receiver. If owners don't engage, the receiver will impose governance.
  • Assessments — the live money issue. The receiver's attorney is expected to move for court approval of (1) a one-time ~$45,000 vegetation-clearing assessment (~$175 each if spread over ~240 parcels) and (2) a monthly maintenance assessment (~$14–19/household). Open questions counsel flagged: are the numbers reasonable, does all the work need doing, who benefits, and how should cost be allocated (should lakefront owners pay more?). Responses will be due about two weeks after the motion is filed.
  • Who pays the case's costs — reserved for trial. The Sept. 2024 decision left "any other matters… determined at trial or upon further hearing": cross-claims for indemnity and contribution, injunctive relief, Water Pollution Control Act claims, and breach-of-Declarations claims. Dismissal of the homeowners, and any fees/fines exposure from the State's and Mullins' claims, are unresolved.
  • Counsel. Eastman & Smith's Motion to Withdraw was filed Sept. 14, 2026 and awaits a court entry. 23 households have signed Mark Long's list to retain substitute counsel — preferably an attorney already in the case — before the Sept. 25 status conference (11:00 a.m.). Unrepresented owners would need to protect their own interests, including any motion for their own dismissal.
  • Insurance. State Farm has not agreed that homeowners/umbrella policies cover the dam claims (the Clarks' test case); no carrier is defending the group.
  • Administrative tail. ODNR final inspection and sign-over of the completed project to the POA; September seeding; the receiver's fee applications; ARPA spend-down deadline Dec. 31, 2026.

D. Open disagreement within the group

Disputed · does the assessment work need a lawyer?

Alex Varughese's position (Sept. 14, answering Matt's "what is left in this process?"): there are two remaining issues. The owner council works with Receiver Harris on bylaws, the ~$45,000 vegetation/reseeding assessment (~$175 across ~240 parcels) and the ~$14–15/month maintenance assessment — "We will not need legal representation for this part." Counsel is needed only for the pending State and Mullins claims and to obtain dismissal.

Counsel's position (Chappelear, Sept. 8 termination letter): the assessments are a court matter, not an HOA housekeeping matter. The receiver's attorney "will be filing a motion soon asking the court to approve assessments for vegetation removal and future maintenance. A written response will be due two weeks later with the court." He lists the questions that response should raise — is the estimate reasonable, could it be done for less, does all the work need doing, who benefits, how should cost be allocated, should those nearest the lake pay more — and warns that the receiver "is not a fiduciary with any duties to the lot owners… If you rely upon him, you do so at your peril."

Why it matters: both can't be right about the same filing. If the receiver's motion is filed while the group is unrepresented, the two-week response window can close with no one objecting to the numbers — and a court-approved assessment is far harder to unwind than a proposed one. This is unresolved within the group as of September 14, with the next status conference on September 25.

Bottom line: nothing more is expected to be litigated about what happens to the dam — that fight is over and built. What remains is who governs, who pays, and how everyone gets out: bylaws, assessments, withdrawal/substitution of counsel, and the reserved claims that stand between the owners and dismissal.
